audio_script: A point on a track needs one number to say where it is. That is one dimension. Give a point a horizontal and vertical coordinate and it can move across a plane: two dimensions. Add depth, and now three coordinates locate it in space. The segment, triangle, and cube are not just drawings with more detail; each uses a different number of independent coordinates. Watch the cube turn: its shape stays rigid while its orientation changes. In the CSV, all three are described by the same geometry primitive, with a dimension, a shape, and optional motion. The renderer embeds one-dimensional coordinates along the x-axis, two-dimensional coordinates in the xy-plane, and three-dimensional coordinates in xyz. This is geometry, not a claim that every physical object is a rigid solid. For curved surfaces or deforming matter, choose a model that supplies the appropriate shape and degrees of freedom.
